plants.name: Coneflower
plants.watering: Water deeply once a week to establish during the first growing season. After that, drought-tolerant — only water during prolonged dry spells. Avoid wet feet, which causes root rot.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun (6+ hours direct light); tolerates light afternoon shade. Prefers well-drained, average soil, not picky on pH (6.0–8.0). Avoid heavy clay or constantly damp spots.
plants.whatToExpect: First year is mostly leafy with maybe a few light blooms. Year 2 onward, expect dense bushy clumps with a generous flush of blooms from June into early fall. 'Cheyenne Spirit' delivers a mix of warm tones — yellow, orange, red, cream, pink — from a single seed packet.
plants.careTips: Deadhead spent blooms to extend flowering. In late fall, leave some seed heads standing for goldfinches and winter interest. Cut back to ground level in early spring. Divide clumps every 3–4 years if they get crowded.
plants.notes: Native to North America. Deer- and rabbit-resistant. Excellent companions: black-eyed Susan, Russian sage, ornamental grasses, salvia.
facts: 'Cheyenne Spirit' won the All-America Selections Gold Medal in 2013, awarded to plants that perform well across many regions.
Echinacea root has a long history of use in Indigenous North American medicine.
Goldfinches and chickadees feast on the seed heads from late fall into winter.
The 'cone' is the prickly central disc — those are hundreds of tiny tubular flowers, not just one.

plants.name: Monarda 'Balmy Lilac'
plants.watering: Likes consistent moisture — water weekly, more in heat. Don't let it dry out completely; mulching helps a lot.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun gives the best blooms; tolerates afternoon shade. Rich, well-drained soil. Slightly acidic to neutral pH.
plants.whatToExpect: Compact, mounded habit (10–12 in tall, much smaller than older 3-ft monardas). Lavender-pink whorled flowers cover the plant in midsummer. Strong minty fragrance from the leaves. Powerful magnet for hummingbirds, bumblebees, and butterflies.
plants.careTips: Deadhead to encourage rebloom. Improve airflow to reduce powdery mildew, a common monarda issue. Cut to ground in fall. Divide every 2–3 years to keep it vigorous.
plants.notes: Native to eastern North America. A member of the mint family — leaves are aromatic and edible (used historically as Oswego tea).
facts: Bee balm is a natural hummingbird magnet; the lavender-pink color is right in their preferred range.
Crush a leaf and you'll smell oregano and mint at once. That's why early Americans used it as a tea substitute.
Native pollinators rely on monarda — over 25 species of bees visit it regularly.
The 'Balmy' series stays under 12 inches, unlike traditional bee balm that can reach 4 feet.

plants.name: Narrow-Leaf Blue Star
plants.watering: Water regularly the first year. Once established, fairly drought-tolerant — water during extended dry spells.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun for best form; gets floppy in too much shade. Tolerates a wide range of soils as long as drainage is decent.
plants.whatToExpect: Soft, feathery foliage like a green cloud all summer. Clusters of pale-blue star-shaped flowers in late spring (about 2–3 weeks). The real showstopper is fall — the entire plant turns brilliant golden yellow. Slow to emerge in spring; be patient.
plants.careTips: Cut back hard (to 6 inches) right after flowering for a tidier mound and less flopping. Doesn't need division — long-lived in place. Stems exude milky sap when cut; can irritate sensitive skin.
plants.notes: Native to the Ouachita Mountains in Arkansas/Oklahoma. Deer-resistant.
facts: Named the Perennial Plant Association's 'Plant of the Year' in 2011, a major honor in the perennial world.
It only really shines twice — pale blue in May, then a stunning gold in October. The summer is just quiet green.
Wild populations are limited to a small region of Arkansas and Oklahoma; it's a relatively recent garden discovery.
Long-lived once established — clumps can persist for decades without needing division.

plants.name: Astilbe 'Hot Pearls'
plants.watering: Loves moisture. Water deeply twice a week, more in hot weather. Mulch helps a lot. Consistent water = strong blooms.
plants.lightSoil: Part shade is ideal — tolerates morning sun and afternoon shade. Rich, moisture-retentive, organic soil. Slightly acidic preferred.
plants.whatToExpect: Glossy fern-like foliage forms a tidy mound. Fluffy plume-shaped flowers rise above the leaves in mid-to-late summer. 'Hot Pearls' has bright pink-coral plumes. More heat- and drought-tolerant than older astilbes thanks to its chinensis parentage.
plants.careTips: Don't let it dry out — wilted leaves brown and may not recover that season. Cut spent flower stalks if you want, or leave for winter interest. Divide every 4 years.
plants.notes: A great pollinator plant despite its delicate appearance. Deer- and rabbit-resistant.
facts: Astilbe chinensis varieties tolerate more sun and dry soil than older Japanese types — 'Hot Pearls' is one of the toughest.
Each plume is hundreds of tiny flowers; the spike is essentially a vertical bouquet.
The name comes from Greek 'a-' (without) and 'stilbe' (brilliance) — 'not shining,' a reference to how dull the individual flowers look up close.

plants.name: Russian Sage 'Prime Time'
plants.watering: Drought-tolerant once established. Water sparingly the first year; barely at all after. Hates wet feet.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun (6+ hrs). Lean, well-drained soil — actually thrives in poor, dry, alkaline conditions. Don't fertilize.
plants.whatToExpect: Compact upright form (unlike older floppy varieties). Silvery, finely-divided aromatic foliage. Long airy spikes of small lavender-blue flowers from mid-summer well into fall. Bee and butterfly magnet.
plants.careTips: Cut back hard in early spring (to 6–10 in) — it blooms on new wood. Don't prune in fall; the silvery stems are nice winter interest. No staking needed for 'Prime Time'.
plants.notes: Despite the common name, it's not a true 'sage' from gardening's classic sense — but botanists recently merged it into Salvia after DNA work.
facts: Despite the name, it's native to Central Asia (the Hindu Kush, Tibet, Iran), not Russia.
Botanists moved it from Perovskia into Salvia in 2017 after DNA studies; it's actually a true sage genetically.
'Prime Time' was bred to stay upright without staking, fixing the main complaint about older Russian sage cultivars.
Bees absolutely cover it in late summer when many other flowers are spent.

plants.name: Cardinal Flower
plants.watering: Loves wet conditions — keep the soil moist at all times. Tolerates standing water. Don't let it dry out in summer.
plants.lightSoil: Tolerates full sun if the soil stays moist; otherwise prefers part shade. Rich, organic, consistently damp soil. Great for rain gardens or pond edges.
plants.whatToExpect: Tall spikes (2–4 ft) of brilliant fire-engine red tubular flowers in late summer. Hummingbird magnet — the red color and tube shape are made for them. Forms basal rosettes that overwinter.
plants.careTips: Mulch heavily to retain moisture. After flowering, cut spent stalks to encourage basal rosettes that become next year's plants. It self-sows; let some seed if you want a sustained colony. Don't bury the rosettes under heavy winter mulch.
plants.notes: Native to the eastern US. Listed as endangered or threatened in several states. Deer-resistant. Short-lived (3–4 years) but reseeds.
facts: Hummingbirds are the primary pollinator — the flower's tube length matches their beak, and most insects can't reach the nectar.
Named 'cardinal' for the brilliant red, matching the robes of Catholic cardinals — first noted by 17th-century European botanists.
All parts are mildly toxic if eaten, which is why deer leave it alone.
Native Americans used it medicinally and ceremonially in many Eastern Woodland cultures.

plants.name: Begonia
plants.watering: Even moisture — water when the top inch dries. Don't soak; bedding begonias rot in soggy soil. Containers may need daily water in heat.
plants.lightSoil: Most begonias (wax / semperflorens) prefer morning sun and afternoon shade or filtered light. Bronze-leaf types take more sun. Rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Containers like a peat-based mix.
plants.whatToExpect: Continuous bloom from late spring until first frost — pink, white, or red flowers depending on variety. Bedding wax begonias make tidy mounds and are essentially carefree. Tuberous types have larger, showier flowers but need more attention.
plants.careTips: Pinch back leggy stems for bushier growth. Deadheading isn't strictly required (most are self-cleaning). Bring indoors before first frost if you want to overwinter (zones 8 and below).
plants.notes: Tender perennial — usually treated as an annual in most US zones. Deer-resistant.
facts: There are over 1,800 species of begonia — one of the largest flowering plant genera.
Begonias were named by Charles Plumier in honor of Michel Bégon, a 17th-century governor of French Haiti and patron of botany.
The leaves are edible and slightly tart, like sorrel — but high in oxalic acid, so only in small amounts.
Native species grow on every continent except Australia and Antarctica.

plants.name: Magnolia
plants.watering: Deep watering once a week the first 2–3 years to establish. Mature magnolias are reasonably drought-tolerant but appreciate water in extended dry spells.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun for most flowering; some tolerate part shade. Rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil. Hates heavy clay paired with drought. Mulch the root zone — magnolias have shallow roots.
plants.whatToExpect: A tree, not a shrub — give it space. Most flowering varieties (saucer, star) bloom before leaves appear with huge cup- or saucer-shaped blooms in white, pink, or purple. Some southern varieties bloom in summer with leathery evergreen leaves. Bloom timing depends on variety.
plants.careTips: Minimal pruning — magnolias don't need it and don't heal pruning wounds well. Remove only dead or damaged branches in early summer. Don't disturb the shallow roots; avoid digging or hard mulching right against the trunk.
plants.notes: Identify your variety to know the bloom time. Saucer magnolia (M. soulangeana) blooms early and is vulnerable to late frosts. Southern magnolia (M. grandiflora) is evergreen and summer-blooming.
facts: Magnolias predate bees. They evolved 95 million years ago and are pollinated by beetles — their tough, waxy petals can take the rough handling.
Magnolia flowers produce no nectar; pollinators come for the pollen.
It's the state flower of Mississippi and Louisiana, and Mississippi's state tree.
Magnolia wood is unusually strong relative to its lightness — historically used for furniture, blinds, and crates.

plants.name: Basil
plants.yield: 1/2–1 cup leaves per plant per week at peak
plants.watering: Water when the top inch dries — about every 2–3 days in summer, daily in heat. Try to water the soil, not the leaves (reduces fungal issues).
plants.lightSoil: Full sun (6+ hrs). Rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost. Doesn't like cold soil — wait until nights are reliably above 50°F to plant out.
plants.whatToExpect: Bushy, fragrant plant. Pinch the growing tips weekly to keep it from flowering and producing leaves. Heavy harvests possible all summer until first frost ends it.
plants.careTips: Pinch flower spikes the moment they appear — once basil flowers, leaf flavor declines and growth slows. Harvest by pinching whole stems above a node — that encourages side branching.
plants.harvestTips: Harvest weekly. Take the top 2–4 leaf pairs of each stem; the plant branches from the cut and grows back fuller. Always cut, don't pluck single leaves. Don't refrigerate cut basil — store stems in water on the counter.
plants.notes: Tender annual — frost will kill it overnight. Considered the 'king of herbs' in Italian cooking; classic with tomatoes (companion plant in the garden too).
facts: Basil and tomato are companion plants in the garden as well as on the plate, thought to deter some tomato pests.
There are over 60 varieties — Genovese, Thai, lemon, cinnamon, holy basil — each with very different flavors.
Holy basil (tulsi) is sacred in Hindu tradition and is grown in many Indian households as a guardian plant.
The name 'basil' comes from the Greek 'basileus' meaning 'king'.

plants.name: Rosemary
plants.watering: Drought-tolerant. Water when soil is dry an inch down. Overwatering kills it faster than anything else.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun (6–8 hrs). Sandy, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil. Hates wet feet. Containers should drain very fast.
plants.whatToExpect: Woody, evergreen shrub in zones 7+. Colder than that, treat as an annual or bring indoors over winter. Fragrant needle-like leaves are usable year-round. Small blue flowers in spring.
plants.careTips: Light pruning to shape after flowering. Don't cut into old woody growth — it doesn't always re-sprout. In cold zones, pot it up and bring inside before first hard frost; place in a sunny window and water sparingly.
plants.harvestTips: Snip 4–6 inch sprigs as needed. Avoid taking more than 1/3 of the plant at a time.
plants.notes: Recently reclassified from Rosmarinus officinalis to Salvia rosmarinus. Deer- and rabbit-resistant. Strong fragrance deters many pests.
facts: Rosemary belongs to the same genus as sage — botanists merged Rosmarinus into Salvia in 2017 after DNA work.
Studies have shown the smell of rosemary improves memory and concentration in test subjects.
It's said to symbolize remembrance — Greek students wore rosemary garlands while studying for exams.
Plants can live 30+ years in the right climate. Some Mediterranean garden shrubs are centuries old.

plants.name: Parsley
plants.yield: A handful of stems per week at peak
plants.watering: Even moisture. Water when the top inch dries — about every 2–3 days in summer. Dries out quickly in containers.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun to part shade (afternoon shade in hot climates). Rich, well-drained soil with organic matter.
plants.whatToExpect: Year 1 — productive, lush green foliage all season. Year 2 — bolts, flowers, sets seed, then dies. For best leaf flavor, treat as an annual and replant each year.
plants.careTips: Snip outer stems first; let new growth emerge from the center. Cut at the base, not just leaves. Once flower stalks appear, leaf flavor declines.
plants.harvestTips: Harvest from the outside in. Use the stems that look ready; new growth from the center keeps coming.
plants.notes: Two main types: flat-leaf (Italian, stronger flavor) and curly (milder, often a garnish). Host plant for black swallowtail butterfly caterpillars — leave a plant for them if you see them.
facts: Black swallowtail butterflies use parsley, dill, and fennel as host plants for their caterpillars. Plant extra if you want to host them.
Parsley is loaded with vitamin K — a tablespoon of fresh leaves has nearly 70% of your daily need.
Ancient Greeks used parsley to crown winners at the Isthmian Games — long before they used it to cook.
Chewing parsley really does freshen breath — the chlorophyll neutralizes some food odors.

plants.name: Cilantro
plants.yield: Quick harvests of leaves; bolts in heat
plants.watering: Even moisture. Water when soil dries an inch down. Mulching helps it last longer in heat.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun in cool weather; part shade in summer to delay bolting. Rich, well-drained, neutral soil.
plants.whatToExpect: Cool-weather herb. Bolts (sends up flower stalks) quickly in heat. Plan for spring and fall harvests, not summer. Once it bolts, leaf flavor changes drastically — but if you let it go to seed, you get coriander from the same plant.
plants.careTips: Sow successively — every 2–3 weeks in spring and fall — for continuous harvest. Don't transplant; cilantro hates root disturbance, sow direct. Pinch flower stalks to delay bolting briefly.
plants.harvestTips: Cut outer stems an inch above the soil. Once it bolts, switch from leaves to seeds — let pods dry on the plant, then harvest the brown seeds.
plants.notes: Some people perceive a soapy taste due to a genetic variant (OR6A2) — biochemistry, not cooking technique.
facts: Some people taste soap when they eat cilantro — tied to a specific gene (OR6A2) that affects how aldehydes are perceived.
Cilantro and coriander are the same plant: leaves are cilantro, seeds are coriander.
Coriander seeds were found in King Tutankhamun's tomb, and references to the plant go back over 7,000 years.
The plant goes from seed to seed in about 100 days — among the fastest-cycling herbs.

plants.name: Blueberry
plants.daysToMaturity: 2–3 years to first real harvest; full production by year 5–6
plants.yield: 5–10 lb per mature bush per year
plants.watering: Consistent moisture is critical — 1–2 inches of water per week. Shallow roots dry out fast. Mulch heavily with pine bark or wood chips.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun (6+ hrs) for best fruit. The big requirement: acidic soil, pH 4.5–5.5. Most yards aren't acidic enough — test before planting and amend with sulfur or pine needles. Sandy, organic, well-drained.
plants.whatToExpect: White or pink bell-shaped flowers in spring → green berries → ripening blue in mid-summer. Don't expect fruit the first 1–2 years (and pinch off any early blooms to put energy into roots). By year 3–5, big harvests. Beautiful red fall foliage. Plant 2+ varieties for cross-pollination — bigger berries.
plants.careTips: Mulch 4–6 inches deep with pine bark or wood chips — keeps soil acidic, holds moisture, suppresses weeds. Net the bush as fruit ripens or birds will strip it. Prune in late winter — remove old canes (>5 years), keep 6–8 strong canes.
plants.harvestTips: Wait — the berry must turn fully blue and slip from the cluster with a gentle touch. If you have to tug, it's not ready. Underripe berries don't sweeten after picking.
plants.notes: One of the few fruits native to North America. Varieties fall into highbush, lowbush, and rabbiteye — make sure yours is suited to your zone.
facts: Blueberries are one of the few major fruits native to North America. Indigenous peoples used them long before European contact.
Their soil pH requirement (4.5–5.5) is the lowest of any common garden fruit — that's why so many home plantings fail.
A mature bush can produce 5–10 pounds of fruit a year and may live 40–50 years if well cared for.
Bumblebees are the main pollinator. Honeybees can do it but blueberry flowers are designed for buzz pollination, which bumbles do better.

plants.name: Roma Tomato
plants.watering: Deep watering 1–2 inches per week — consistency matters more than total amount. Inconsistent water causes blossom-end rot and cracking. Water at the soil level, not on leaves (reduces blight).
plants.lightSoil: Full sun (8+ hours ideal). Rich, well-drained soil, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8). Amend with compost.
plants.whatToExpect: Determinate variety — bushy, semi-compact, sets fruit over a 2–3 week window then mostly stops. Egg-shaped, meaty, low-juice fruits about 2–3 oz each. Best for sauce, paste, and canning. Cluster fruit ripens together.
plants.careTips: Stake or cage at planting time. Mulch heavily once soil warms. Pinch lower suckers if you want bigger fruit; determinate types don't need much suckering. Side-dress with compost or fish emulsion mid-season. Watch for hornworms (big green caterpillars) and remove by hand.
plants.harvestTips: Pick when fully red — Romas don't deepen flavor much off the vine. Twist, don't pull. Refrigerating ruins texture; ripen and store on the counter.
plants.notes: Determinate, so not as sprawling as indeterminate varieties — but still needs support. Resistant to verticillium and fusarium wilt (look for VFN tags).
facts: Romas are the gold standard sauce tomato — meaty, low water, dense fruit. Slicing tomatoes (beefsteaks) are too wet for sauce.
Romas were developed in 1955 at the USDA, bred specifically for paste and canning.
Determinate tomatoes set all their fruit in a 2–3 week window — handy if you want a big batch for canning at once.
Tomatoes are technically a fruit (a berry, botanically), but the US Supreme Court ruled them a vegetable in 1893 for tariff purposes.

plants.name: California Wonder Pepper
plants.watering: Even moisture, 1–2 inches per week. Inconsistent water → blossom-end rot. Mulch helps.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun (8+ hrs ideal). Rich, well-drained soil with plenty of organic matter. Loves warm soil — wait until nights are above 60°F.
plants.whatToExpect: Compact bushy plants. 4-lobed blocky bell peppers ~4 inches across, 4 inches tall. Start green; left on the plant they ripen to red and gain sweetness. Heaviest fruit set in mid-to-late summer.
plants.careTips: Stake or cage as fruit weight pulls plants over. Pinch off the first flowers if the plant is small to redirect energy to roots. Side-dress with balanced fertilizer when blooms start. Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizer or you'll get all leaves and no fruit.
plants.harvestTips: Cut peppers off with shears or a knife — pulling can break stems. Pick at any size you like; let some go red for sweeter flavor.
plants.notes: Heirloom variety, introduced in 1928. Disease resistance is moderate.
facts: California Wonder is one of the most popular bell peppers in the US — introduced in 1928 and still going strong.
Bell peppers contain zero capsaicin — a quirk of recessive genetics within Capsicum annuum, the same species as jalapeños and cayennes.
A red bell has about 3× the vitamin C of an orange, and twice as much as a green one of the same variety (vitamin C builds with ripening).
Peppers are perennial in their native tropics; they're treated as annuals only because frost kills them.

plants.name: Snap Beans
plants.yield: 1/2–1 lb per bush plant; more from pole types
plants.watering: Even moisture once flowering starts. Don't overwater seedlings. Avoid wetting foliage to reduce disease.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun (6+ hrs). Average, well-drained soil. Beans fix their own nitrogen — don't fertilize with high-N feeds; you'll get leaves and few beans.
plants.whatToExpect: Direct-sow after frost — beans hate transplanting. White flowers, then beans 7–10 days later. Bush varieties produce a heavy first flush; pole varieties produce continuously until frost. Pick often for more production.
plants.careTips: Sow successively every 2 weeks for ongoing harvest from bush types. Pole beans need a 6+ ft trellis. Inoculate seeds with rhizobium bacteria for better nitrogen fixation in poor soil. Watch for Mexican bean beetles and aphids.
plants.harvestTips: Pick when pods are firm and the seeds inside are still small — you should be able to snap a pod cleanly in half. Pick every 2–3 days to keep flowers coming. Overripe pods slow further production.
plants.notes: Beans fix atmospheric nitrogen via root bacteria — improves soil fertility for the next crop. Excellent rotation crop.
facts: Beans, corn, and squash are the 'Three Sisters' — a Native American companion planting where beans climb the corn and fix nitrogen for the squash.
Bean roots host Rhizobium bacteria that pull atmospheric nitrogen into the soil. They literally fertilize themselves and the next year's crop.
The 'snap' in snap beans came from how a fresh pod breaks crisply in half.
Phaseolus vulgaris originated in Central and South America; the species includes green beans, kidney beans, navy beans, and pintos — all the same plant.

plants.name: Valencia Orange Pepper
plants.watering: Even moisture, 1–2 inches per week. Mulch helps.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun (8+ hrs). Rich, well-drained soil. Loves heat.
plants.whatToExpect: Compact plants with 4-lobed blocky bell peppers that ripen from green to bright orange. Sweet, juicy, slightly fruitier than red bells. Starts producing in mid-summer.
plants.careTips: Stake or cage as fruit ripens. Pinch first flowers if plant is small. Don't over-fertilize with nitrogen.
plants.harvestTips: Wait for full orange color for best flavor — sweetness peaks at the orange stage. Cut with shears.
plants.notes: One of several 'color varieties' of bell pepper sold for variety in the garden. Care is identical to other bells.
facts: Orange bells are sweeter than green and have more beta-carotene — visually bright peppers tend to have higher antioxidant content.
All bell pepper colors are the same species; the variety determines what color it ripens to (red, yellow, orange, chocolate brown, even purple).
Orange peppers contain zeaxanthin, a carotenoid linked to eye health.

plants.name: Jalapeño
plants.watering: 1–1.5 inches per week. Mild water stress can actually increase heat — don't over-pamper.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun (8+ hrs). Rich, well-drained soil. Warm-soil lover; wait until nights are above 55°F.
plants.whatToExpect: Bushy, productive plant. Glossy green tapered fruits 2–3 inches long. Picked green is the standard; left on the vine they turn red and sweeten slightly while gaining heat. Heat: 2,500–8,000 SHU (Scoville).
plants.careTips: Stake taller plants. Heat varies with weather and stress — drought + heat = hotter peppers. Side-dress with balanced fertilizer when flowering. Pick frequently to keep plants producing.
plants.harvestTips: Cut with shears (snapping can break the stem). Wear gloves if you handle a lot — capsaicin transfers to skin and stays.
plants.notes: Most popular hot pepper in the US. Mild compared to other chiles but still spicy. Smoked + dried jalapeños = chipotles.
facts: Smoked, dried jalapeños are chipotles — the same plant in another form.
Heat is in the white pith and seeds, not the flesh. Remove the pith to lower heat.
Jalapeños with corky brown lines ('corking') are usually hotter — those lines indicate stress during ripening.
Named after Xalapa, the capital of Veracruz, Mexico — historically the trading center for them.

plants.name: Serrano Pepper
plants.watering: 1–1.5 inches per week. Mulch.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun (8+ hrs). Rich, well-drained soil, slightly acidic. Warm soil only — wait until nights above 55°F.
plants.whatToExpect: Tall bushy plant — taller than jalapeños. Slim tapered green fruits ~2 inches long, ripening to red, brown, orange, or yellow depending on variety. Heat: 10,000–25,000 SHU — about 3–5× a jalapeño.
plants.careTips: Stake — they get tall and laden with fruit. Same care as jalapeños otherwise. Watch for aphids on new growth.
plants.harvestTips: Most often used green. Wear gloves — they're noticeably hotter than jalapeños and capsaicin lingers on skin.
plants.notes: Native to the mountain regions of Puebla and Hidalgo, Mexico. Essential in salsa fresca and pico de gallo.
facts: Serranos are 3–5× hotter than jalapeños on the Scoville scale.
Named for the sierras (mountain regions) of Puebla and Hidalgo in Mexico, where they originated.
Typically used green — they're rarely sold red despite ripening to red.
A single serrano plant can produce 50+ peppers in a good year.

plants.name: Chili Pepper
plants.watering: About 1 inch per week. Moderate water stress can intensify heat.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun (8+ hrs). Rich, well-drained soil. Warmth-loving.
plants.whatToExpect: 'Chili pepper' is a category, not a single variety, so specifics are hard. Most 'chili pepper' plants from a nursery are cayenne-type — slim red 4–6 inch fruits, drying easily for chili powder. Heat: cayenne is ~30,000–50,000 SHU.
plants.careTips: Standard hot pepper care. Stake taller plants. Don't over-fertilize with nitrogen. Allow fruits to ripen fully red for drying.
plants.harvestTips: Cut with shears. Wear gloves. To dry: pick fully ripe red fruits and string them up in a dry, airy spot.
plants.notes: Once you know the actual variety from the original tag, update this entry — care can vary.
facts: 'Chili pepper' covers thousands of varieties across the genus Capsicum. Most home-garden 'chili' plants are cayenne-type.
Capsaicin (the heat compound) doesn't actually burn anything — it triggers the same receptors that respond to heat, fooling the brain.
Capsicum is native to Central and South America; chiles spread worldwide after Columbus, transforming cuisines globally in 200 years.
Birds can't taste capsaicin — that's evolution: birds spread the seeds intact, mammals would crush them.

plants.name: Green Pepper
plants.watering: Even moisture, 1–2 inches per week.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun. Rich, well-drained soil.
plants.whatToExpect: Variety unknown — likely a generic green bell sold for being picked at the green stage. Most box-store 'green pepper' plants behave like California Wonder. Bushy plant with blocky 3–4 inch peppers.
plants.careTips: Stake or cage as needed. Pinch first flowers if plant is small. Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizer.
plants.harvestTips: Pick at the green stage when peppers feel firm and have reached full size. If you let them stay on the plant, most will turn red and sweeten — but yields drop because the plant invests in ripening.
plants.notes: Variety wasn't recorded — look at the original plant tag if possible. Care identical to California Wonder unless the variety is known to differ.
facts: Most 'green peppers' are just unripe bell peppers picked early. If you let them ripen, they almost always turn red and become noticeably sweeter.
Green bells have about 1/3 the vitamin C of red bells of the same variety — the vitamin C builds with ripening.
Some varieties (like 'Permagreen') stay green even when fully ripe — those are the exception, not the rule.

plants.name: Red Pepper
plants.watering: Even moisture, 1–2 inches per week.
plants.lightSoil: Full sun. Rich, well-drained soil.
plants.whatToExpect: Variety unknown — likely a red-ripening bell variety. The plant produces green peppers first, which deepen to red over 2–3 weeks on the vine. Sweeter than peppers picked green. Yield is typically lower because the plant invests more energy in ripening each fruit.
plants.careTips: Patience — leaving fruit on the plant to fully redden takes extra time. Stake to support the heavier ripe fruit. Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizer.
plants.harvestTips: Wait for full red color. The pepper should feel firm and the color should be uniform. Cut with shears.
plants.notes: Variety wasn't recorded. Likely a red bell variety such as 'Red Beauty' or 'Lady Bell'. Care is identical to other bells.
facts: A red bell pepper has roughly twice the vitamin C and 8× the vitamin A of a green one of the same variety — color gain comes with nutrient gain.
Red bells take 2–3 weeks longer than green bells of the same plant — patience for sweetness.
The red color comes from beta-carotene and lycopene — the same antioxidants in carrots and tomatoes.
